common_name: Akila Daisy White Osteospermum (Uniform-Flowering African Daisy)

planting.note: Set out rooted plants once nights stay above 45°F; this series is bred to open flowers within a tight window, so uniform planting dates give the most even bedding display.

directions: Plant in fast-draining soil and avoid overhead watering, which can spot the petals and invite botrytis. Shear lightly after the first big flush to encourage a tighter, more floriferous mound rather than deadheading spent blooms one by one. This cultivar tolerates heat and dry spells better than older seed lines but still benefits from a light monthly feed during peak bloom.

planting.note: Transplant after frost danger passes into containers or borders where the bronzy-orange, pink-centered flowers can be seen up close.

directions: Give this compact selection excellent drainage, since Serenity-type Osteospermum sulk and drop buds in soggy soil. Flowers close on overcast days and at night, so plant where the closed-bud form still reads as tidy rather than bare. Pinch young plants once to promote branching, and expect a rebloom flush after a midsummer trim.

common_name: Serenity White Osteospermum (Pure White Compact African Daisy)

planting.note: Move plants outdoors once temperatures stabilize above freezing; bright white blooms show best against dark mulch or foliage backdrops.

directions: This compact white form performs best in lean, well-drained soil with consistent but light moisture rather than heavy irrigation. Deadhead spent flower stems at the base to keep the mound looking clean, since faded blooms brown noticeably against the white petals. Reduce feeding in high heat, when growth naturally slows and flower count dips.

common_name: FlowerPower Spider White Osteospermum (Spoon-Petaled African Daisy)

planting.note: Set out after frost into a spot with room to spread, since the spoon-shaped petals show best on a plant allowed to fill out rather than being crowded.

directions: The quilled, spoon-tipped petals of this FlowerPower series selection hold up well in wind and light rain compared with flat-petaled daisies, but the plant still wants sharp drainage to avoid root rot. Cut back stems by a third in midsummer if flowering slows, which typically triggers a strong fall flush. Grow it as a container spiller or warm-climate perennial where winters stay mild.

common_name: FlowerPower Spider Purple Osteospermum (Spoon-Petaled African Daisy)

planting.note: Plant out after frost danger passes; the deep purple, spoon-petaled flowers pair well with silver or chartreuse foliage companions.

directions: Give this FlowerPower series cultivar full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, since the curled petal form is more prone to fungal spotting in humid, still air than standard daisy types. Trim back hard after the first bloom cycle to reset the plant's shape and stimulate fresh growth. It roots easily from tip cuttings taken in late summer for overwintering indoors.

common_name: Zion Copper Amethyst Osteospermum (Multi-Toned African Daisy)

planting.note: Transplant into full sun after the last frost; the layered copper, pink, and purple tones look best planted in drifts rather than singly.

directions: This earth-toned selection forms a tight mound that needs little staking, but it flowers most heavily when watered deeply and infrequently rather than kept constantly moist. Remove faded flower stems to prevent seed set, which otherwise diverts energy from new buds. It tolerates poor, sandy soils better than richer garden loam, where excess nitrogen can push foliage over flowers.

common_name: Zion Purple Sun Osteospermum (Vivid Purple African Daisy)

planting.note: Set out after frost risk ends; the saturated purple flowers with a yellow-gold eye read well from a distance in mass plantings.

directions: Like other Zion-series daisies, this cultivar wants sharp drainage and dislikes wet feet, so raised beds or amended containers suit it well. Blooms close in low light, so site it where afternoon sun keeps flowers open longer into the evening. A light shearing once flowering tapers in midsummer heat renews the display for autumn.

common_name: Blue Eyed Beauty Osteospermum (Yellow African Daisy with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant after frost into slopes, walls, or containers where its spreading habit can cascade; it is useful for erosion control on sunny banks.

directions: The lemon-yellow petals and blue-purple eye stand out best against dark mulch or evergreen backdrops, so consider placement before planting. This spreading cultivar roots where trailing stems touch soil, which can be used to fill in bare patches along a border edge. Keep soil on the dry side between waterings, since constantly damp roots shorten the plant's life in warm climates.

planting.note: Set out after frost passes; the ridged, double-layered silvery-mauve blooms benefit from extra spacing so each flower's texture is visible.

directions: The doubled, ridge-petaled flowers of this series are heavier than single-form daisies, so plant in a spot sheltered from strong wind to prevent stem flop. Water at the base rather than overhead to keep the layered petals from trapping moisture and developing gray mold. This cultivar branches readily, so a single early pinch is usually enough to build a full, well-rounded plant.

common_name: Bright Lights Purple Osteospermum (Heat-Tolerant African Daisy)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into full sun; this selection was bred for better summer heat performance than older Osteospermum lines, so it can go in earlier warm beds.

directions: This heat-tolerant selection holds its large purple flowers upright even in summer conditions that cause older Osteospermum varieties to fade or flop. Water deeply but let the top inch of soil dry between waterings to prevent root disease. Deadhead regularly during peak season to keep the mounded habit blooming continuously rather than setting seed.

common_name: New Day White Gazania (Early-Flowering Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Set out after frost danger passes into a hot, dry site; this series was bred to flower earlier and more uniformly than older seed strains.

directions: Grow this low clumping form in lean, gritty soil, since rich or constantly moist ground produces lush foliage at the expense of flowers. Blooms close on cloudy days and at dusk, reopening fully only in direct sun, so avoid shaded plantings. Removing spent flower stalks at their base keeps the compact mound tidy and encourages continuous rebloom through summer heat.

common_name: New Day Bronze Shades Gazania (Earthy-Toned Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Transplant after frost into full sun and reflected-heat spots like gravel gardens or curbside strips, where the bronze tones read especially well.

directions: This drought-tough selection thrives on neglect once established and rots quickly if kept too wet, so err toward underwatering. The silvery, felted foliage adds interest even when flowers close in shade or evening, making it useful as a groundcover edge. Shear lightly midseason if plants become sparse in the center to renew flowering from the crown.

common_name: Big Kiss Red Gazania (Large-Flowered Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Set out after the last frost into a sunny bed or large container; the oversized mahogany-red blooms need a bit more elbow room than standard gazanias.

directions: This large-flowered selection needs consistently sharp drainage, since its bigger blooms and broader leaves can trap moisture and invite crown rot in heavy soil. Deadhead the sizable flower stems promptly to keep new buds coming rather than letting the plant set seed. It performs best in reflected heat, such as along a sidewalk or south-facing wall, where flower size and color intensify.

common_name: Big Kiss White Flame Gazania (Striped Large-Flowered Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Plant out after frost into full sun; the bold white-and-rose striping on oversized flowers is most vivid when plants get uninterrupted afternoon light.

directions: Give this striped, large-flowered form the same lean, fast-draining conditions as other treasure flowers, since fertile soil dilutes bloom color and stripe contrast. Water at soil level in the morning so foliage dries quickly and flowers stay open through the afternoon. Remove tattered older leaves at the base periodically to keep air moving through the clump in humid weather.

common_name: Daybreak Red Stripe Gazania (Striped Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Transplant after frost into a hot, sunny spot; the golden-yellow petals with a bold central red stripe show best massed together as edging.

directions: This compact, early-blooming selection is well suited to edging or rock gardens where its striped flowers can be viewed at close range. Keep watering infrequent and deep rather than frequent and shallow, since shallow moisture encourages weak roots and fewer flowers. Trim back any leggy stems in late summer to keep the low mound compact through fall.

common_name: Daybreak Bright Orange Gazania (Vivid Orange Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Set out after the last frost into full sun; the saturated orange flowers make a strong edging or groundcover statement in hot, dry beds.

directions: Like other members of this compact series, it flowers most heavily in poor, well-drained soil and full, unobstructed sun. Avoid mulching too close to the crown, which can hold moisture against the base and encourage rot in humid climates. Once established, this cultivar tolerates short dry spells better than most bedding annuals, making it a good choice for low-maintenance borders.

common_name: Colorado Gold Gazania (Cold-Hardy Trailing Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Transplant into gritty, well-drained soil after frost; unlike bedding gazanias, this species is winter-hardy in much colder climates and can be treated as a perennial groundcover.

directions: This narrow-leaved species spreads into a low, glossy mat that spills nicely over walls or container edges, unlike the clumping habit of common bedding gazanias. It needs lean, sharply drained soil to survive winter wet, which is the main threat to its cold hardiness rather than the cold itself. Established plantings need almost no supplemental water once roots are settled, and shearing spent flower stems after the main spring flush encourages sporadic rebloom into fall.
